title: Aeacus. Pestilentia. Myrmidones
titleEn: Minos at Aegina, and the Plague — Metamorphoses VII.453–551
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Minos gathers allies island by island for a war of vengeance for his son Androgeos and comes to Aegina, where Aeacus refuses him: no land is bound closer to Athens than this one. In the same hour an Athenian ship puts in with Cephalus aboard, who asks for aid and is told not to ask for it but to take it; and when Cephalus misses many faces he remembers from an earlier visit, Aeacus tells him how a plague sent by Juno's anger came on the island, killing the animals first and leaving bodies lying in the woods and fields that not even wolves would touch.

sentences.t:
Nec tamen (usque adeo nulla est sincera voluptas,
sollicitumque aliquid laetis intervenit) Aegeus
gaudia percepit nato secura recepto.
sentences.l: And yet not — so utterly is no pleasure unmixed, and something anxious comes between glad things — did Aegeus take joys free from care, his son having been recovered.
sentences.i: And yet Aegeus did not take an untroubled joy in the recovery of his son — so true it is that no pleasure is unmixed, and something anxious slips in among our joys.
sentences.n: The parenthesis is a sententia, a general truth dropped into the story: Ovid interrupts his own sentence to state it and then finishes the sentence. "nato ... recepto" is an ablative absolute, a self-contained "with X done" phrase where English wants a clause; secura goes with gaudia, so the joys, not the son, are the untroubled thing.

sentences.t: Bella parat Minos.
sentences.l: Minos prepares wars.
sentences.i: Minos is making ready for war.
sentences.n: Three words, set off by themselves, and the narrative turns. The plural bella is ordinary Latin for a single campaign, and the present tense is the historic present, which puts the action in front of the reader as if it were happening now.

sentences.t:
Qui quamquam milite, quamquam
classe valet, patria tamen est firmissimus ira
Androgeique necem iustis ulciscitur armis.
sentences.l: And he, although he is strong in soldiery, although in fleet, is nevertheless strongest in a father's anger, and avenges the killing of Androgeos with just arms.
sentences.i: Strong though he is in troops and strong in ships, his greatest strength is a father's anger, and he avenges the killing of Androgeos with arms he holds to be just.
sentences.n: Qui opens the sentence as a connecting relative — "and he", not "who". miles is a collective singular, the soldiery rather than one soldier. patria ira is "a father's anger" (from pater), not "native"; Androgeos was Minos's son, and iustis is Minos's own verdict on his war, not the poem's.

sentences.t:
Ante tamen bello vires adquirit amicas,
quaque potens habitus, volucri freta classe pererrat.
sentences.l: But first he acquires friendly forces for the war, and wherever he was held powerful, he roves over the straits with his flying fleet.
sentences.i: But first he gathers allied strength for the war, ranging the straits with his swift fleet wherever his power was acknowledged.
sentences.n: freta is not the participle fretus, "relying on", but the neuter plural noun "straits", and it is the object of pererrat; the fleet is in the ablative. "quaque potens habitus" leaves out the verb "to be": habitus (est) means "he was held, considered". volucer, "winged", is a standing epithet for speed.

sentences.t:
Hinc Anaphen sibi iungit et Astypaleia regna,
promissis Anaphen, regna Astypaleia bello;
sentences.l: From here he joins Anaphe to himself and the Astypalaean realms — Anaphe by promises, the Astypalaean realms by war.
sentences.i: Here he wins over Anaphe and the kingdom of Astypalaea — Anaphe by promises, Astypalaea by war.
sentences.n: The second line takes the two names of the first in the same order and gives each its means, promises or force. Anaphen keeps its Greek accusative ending, as many of the island names in this catalogue do. Anaphe and Astypalaea are small islands of the southern Aegean.

sentences.t:
hinc humilem Myconum cretosaque rura Cimoli
florentemque thymo Cythnum parvamque Seriphon
marmoreamque Paron,
sentences.l: from here low Myconos and the chalky fields of Cimolus, and Cythnos flowering with thyme, and small Seriphos, and marble Paros,
sentences.i: next low-lying Myconos and the chalk country of Cimolus, Cythnos in flower with thyme, little Seriphos, marble Paros,
sentences.n: The verb iungit is still doing the work three lines on; the catalogue is a chain of accusatives hung on it. Each island gets one epithet and no more: Cimolian earth was quarried as a cleaning chalk, and Parian marble was the finest known. Magnus prints Cythnum parvamque; some editions read "Syron planamque", making the island Syros and the epithet "flat" for Seriphos.

sentences.t:
quaque impia prodidit Arnen
Sithonis
sentences.l: and where the impious Sithonian woman betrayed Arne
sentences.i: and the place where an impious Thracian woman betrayed Arne
sentences.n: quaque is the ablative of place, "and where", not a form of quisque. Sithonis is a feminine adjective standing alone as a noun, "the Sithonian", that is the Thracian, woman. Magnus prints Arnen as the thing betrayed; some editions read "Arne, Siphnon", which makes Arne herself the traitor and Siphnos the island she sold.

sentences.t:
(accepto, quod avara poposcerat, auro
mutata est in avem,
sentences.l: (the gold having been received which, greedy, she had demanded, she was changed into a bird,
sentences.i: (once she had taken the gold her greed had demanded, she was turned into a bird,
sentences.n: "accepto ... auro" is an ablative absolute pulled apart, with its own relative clause wedged inside it — the noun waits three words past its participle. avara is a nominative adjective doing adverbial work: she demanded the gold in her greed.

sentences.t:
quae nunc quoque diligit aurum,
nigra pedes, nigris velata monedula pennis).
sentences.l: which even now loves gold — a jackdaw black as to her feet, veiled with black feathers).
sentences.i: a bird that loves gold to this day: the jackdaw, black-footed and cloaked in black plumage.
sentences.n: "nigra pedes" is a Greek accusative of respect — black in respect of her feet — a construction Latin poets borrow from Greek, where English needs "as to" or a compound like "black-footed". Here quoque is the adverb "also, even", not the ablative quo-que "and with which". The jackdaw's reputation for carrying off anything bright is the point of the punishment.

sentences.t:
At non Oliaros Didymaeque et Tenos et Andros
et Gyaros nitidaeque ferax Peparethos olivae
Gnosiacas iuvere rates.
sentences.l: But Oliaros and the Didymae and Tenos and Andros and Gyaros and Peparethos, fruitful of glossy olive, did not help the Cnossian ships.
sentences.i: But Oliaros, the Didymae, Tenos, Andros, Gyaros, and Peparethos rich in glossy olives gave the Cretan ships no help.
sentences.n: iuvere is iuverunt, the poetic third-person plural perfect in -ere; it comes several times more in these lines, and the ending is easy to mistake for an infinitive. ferax takes the genitive, "fruitful of". Gnosiacus means "of Cnossos", the great city of Crete, and so simply "Cretan": these are Minos's ships.

sentences.t:
Latere inde sinistro
Oenopiam Minos petit, Aeacideia regna:
sentences.l: From there, on the left side, Minos makes for Oenopia, the realms of Aeacus:
sentences.i: From there, keeping the land on his left, Minos makes for Oenopia, the kingdom of Aeacus.
sentences.n: "latere sinistro" is an ablative of the route taken, the ship's course reckoned by which side the land lies on. Aeacideius is an adjective formed from the name Aeacus. regna is a poetic plural: one kingdom, not several.

sentences.t:
Oenopiam veteres appellavere, sed ipse
Aeacus Aeginam genetricis nomine dixit.
sentences.l: The men of old called it Oenopia, but Aeacus himself named it Aegina, by his mother's name.
sentences.i: The ancients called it Oenopia, but Aeacus himself called it Aegina, after his mother.
sentences.n: appellavere is again -ere for -erunt. The island therefore carries the name of a woman, Aeacus's mother — which is what makes the bitter phrase at 524, "lands named after the mistress", land where it does. dixit here means "called", with a double accusative: called it Aegina.

sentences.t:
Turba ruit tantaeque virum cognoscere famae
expetit.
sentences.l: The crowd rushes up and seeks to know a man of such great fame.
sentences.i: The crowd comes running, eager to meet a man of such renown.
sentences.n: "virum tantae famae" is a genitive of description, the quality attached to the noun as English attaches it with "of": a man of such fame. turba is a collective singular and takes singular verbs, ruit and expetit, though it is a great many people.

sentences.t:
Occurrunt illi Telamonque, minorque
quam Telamon Peleus, et proles tertia Phocus.
sentences.l: Telamon runs to meet him, and Peleus, younger than Telamon, and the third offspring, Phocus.
sentences.i: Telamon comes out to meet him, and Peleus, younger than Telamon, and the third son, Phocus.
sentences.n: occurro takes the dative of the person met, illi. The three are Aeacus's sons, and the line ranks them by age as it names them; proles is a neuter-sounding but feminine noun for offspring, used here of a man.

sentences.t:
Ipse quoque egreditur tardus gravitate senili
Aeacus, et quae sit veniendi causa requirit.
sentences.l: Aeacus himself too comes out, slow with the heaviness of old age, and asks what the cause of the coming is.
sentences.i: Aeacus himself comes out as well, slowed by the weight of his years, and asks what has brought his visitor.
sentences.n: egreditur is deponent: passive in form, active in meaning — he comes out, he is not brought out. "quae sit ... causa" is an indirect question and so takes the subjunctive, where the direct question would have est. veniendi is a gerund in the genitive, "of coming".

sentences.t:
Admonitus patrii luctus suspirat et illi
dicta refert rector populorum talia centum:
sentences.l: Reminded of a father's grief, the ruler of a hundred peoples sighs and brings back to him such words as these:
sentences.i: Reminded of his grief as a father, the ruler of a hundred peoples sighs, and gives him this answer:
sentences.n: admonitus takes the genitive of the thing recalled. The one who sighs is the visitor, Minos, named not by name but by his title: Crete was famous as the island of a hundred cities. "dicta refert" is "brings words back", the ordinary way of saying "replies".

sentences.t:
“Arma iuves oro pro gnato sumpta piaeque
pars sis militiae; tumulo solacia posco.”
sentences.l: "I beg you help arms taken up for a son, and be a part of a dutiful campaign: I ask consolations for a tomb."
sentences.i: "Help, I beg, the arms I have taken up for my son, and be part of a righteous war: what I ask is comfort for a grave."
sentences.n: oro governs the bare subjunctives iuves and sis with no ut, a compact construction common in verse: "I beg that you help". gnato is an older spelling of nato, kept by this edition. The campaign is pia because a father owes it to a dead son; pietas is duty owed to family and gods, and it is the word that justifies the whole war.

sentences.t:
Huic Asopiades “petis inrita” dixit “et urbi
non facienda meae:
sentences.l: To him the descendant of Asopus said, "You ask for things that are void, and not to be done by my city:
sentences.i: The descendant of Asopus answered him: "What you ask is null, and my city cannot do it.
sentences.n: Asopiades is a patronymic for Aeacus: his mother Aegina was daughter of the river-god Asopus, so the name says the same thing the island's name says. inrita (this edition's spelling of irrita) is neuter plural, "of no effect, not ratified" — the word belongs to treaties and votes. facienda is a gerundive of obligation with urbi meae as the dative of the agent: things my city must not do.

sentences.t:
neque enim coniunctior ulla
Cecropidis hac est tellus: ea foedera nobis.”
sentences.l: for no land is more joined to the sons of Cecrops than this one: such are our treaties."
sentences.i: for no country is bound closer to the people of Cecrops than this: that is what our treaties are."
sentences.n: The Cecropidae are the Athenians, named from Cecrops, their first king; the dative goes with coniunctior, and hac is an ablative of comparison, "than this". The last clause has no verb at all — "those, our treaties" — and the bluntness is the refusal.

sentences.t:
Tristis abit “stabunt” que “tibi tua foedera magno”
dixit
sentences.l: Grim he goes away, and "your treaties," he said, "will stand you at a great price,"
sentences.i: He leaves grim-faced, with a parting word: "These treaties of yours will cost you dear,"
sentences.n: "stare" with an ablative of price is a merchant's idiom — a thing stands you at so much, it costs you so much — and the threat is that Aegina will pay for its loyalty. tristis is an adjective where English wants an adverb, describing the man rather than the going. The edition prints the enclitic que as a separate word here because the quotation marks come between it and stabunt.

sentences.t:
et utilius bellum putat esse minari
quam gerere atque suas ibi praeconsumere vires.
sentences.l: and he thinks it more useful to threaten war than to wage it and to use up his forces there beforehand.
sentences.i: and he judges it more profitable to threaten war than to wage it and spend his strength there in advance.
sentences.n: "utilius esse" heads an indirect statement whose subject is the infinitive minari itself: that to threaten is more useful. praeconsumere is a rare compound, "to use up ahead of time"; ibi means at Aegina, before he has even reached Athens.

sentences.t:
Classis ab Oenopiis etiamnum Lyctia muris
spectari poterat, cum pleno concita velo
Attica puppis adest in portusque intrat amicos,
sentences.l: The Lyctian fleet could still be seen from the Oenopian walls, when an Attic ship, driven on with full sail, is there and enters friendly harbours,
sentences.i: The Cretan fleet could still be seen from the walls of Oenopia when an Athenian ship, running under full sail, arrives and puts in to a friendly harbour,
sentences.n: Lyctos was a town of Crete, so "Lyctian" means Cretan, as "Attic" means Athenian. The cum clause carries the main event rather than the subordinate one — the imperfect sets the scene and the present adest cuts into it. puppis is strictly the stern, standing for the whole ship, and portus is a poetic plural for one harbour.

sentences.t: quae Cephalum patriaeque simul mandata ferebat.
sentences.l: which was carrying Cephalus and at the same time the commissions of his fatherland.
sentences.i: carrying Cephalus and his country's charge together.
sentences.n: One verb, ferebat, carries a man and an abstract at once, which is a figure Latin likes and English resists. mandata are the instructions an envoy is given and must deliver; the word returns at 502 when he delivers them.

sentences.t:
Aeacidae longo iuvenes post tempore visum
agnovere tamen Cephalum dextrasque dedere
inque patris duxere domum.
sentences.l: The young sons of Aeacus recognised Cephalus nevertheless, seen after a long time, and gave right hands and led him into their father's house.
sentences.i: Aeacus' sons, young as they were, knew Cephalus even so, though it was long since they had seen him; they gave him their hands and led him into their father's house.
sentences.n: Three perfects in -ere in two lines — agnovere, dedere, duxere — all for -erunt. "longo post tempore" has the preposition displaced inside its own phrase, a common poetic licence. Giving the right hand is the formal act of welcome and of pledge, not a casual greeting.

sentences.t:
Spectabilis heros
et veteris retinens etiamnum pignera formae
ingreditur
sentences.l: The hero, worth looking at and still keeping the pledges of his old beauty, walks in,
sentences.i: The hero walks in, still striking, still holding the tokens of his former beauty,
sentences.n: forma here is beauty, not shape. pignera (some editions spell it pignora) are pledges or securities, what is left behind as proof — the traces of what he was. etiamnum, "even now", quietly says how long ago that was.

sentences.t:
ramumque tenens popularis olivae
a dextra laevaque duos aetate minores
maior habet, Clyton et Buten, Pallante creatos.
sentences.l: and holding a branch of his people's olive he, the elder, has on his right and left two younger in age, Clytos and Butes, begotten of Pallas.
sentences.i: and carrying a branch of his city's olive, the elder man has on either side two younger than himself, Clytos and Butes, sons of Pallas.
sentences.n: The olive is Athens's own tree, and a branch carried in the hand marks a man who comes to ask. popularis is "of his people", not "popular". "Pallante creatos" is an ablative of origin, born from Pallas; and maior against minores sets the one man's age against the two, which is the whole picture of the group.

sentences.t: Postquam congressus primi sua verba tulerunt,
sentences.l: After the first meetings had brought their own words,
sentences.i: When the first exchange had produced the words that belong to it,
sentences.n: congressus is a fourth-declension plural, the first encounters. "sua verba" are the words proper to such an occasion — the greetings a meeting has to get through before anything can be said. The line is Ovid's way of skipping the courtesies without pretending they did not happen.

sentences.t:
Cecropidae Cephalus peragit mandata rogatque
auxilium foedusque refert et iura parentum
imperiumque peti totius Achaidos addit.
sentences.l: Cephalus carries out the Cecropid's commission and asks for aid, and recalls the treaty and the rights of their fathers, and adds that the rule of all Achaia is being sought.
sentences.i: Cephalus discharges the Athenian king's commission: he asks for aid, invokes the treaty and the rights their fathers held, and adds that what is being sought is dominion over the whole of Greece.
sentences.n: Cecropidae is a genitive singular, "of the son of Cecrops", the king of Athens who sent him. peragere is to carry a thing through to its end, so to deliver a message in full. "imperium peti" is an indirect statement with a passive infinitive that names no agent — Minos is left unspoken. Achaidos is a Greek genitive; Achaia stands for Greece at large.

sentences.l: So, when eloquence had helped the entrusted cause, Aeacus, with his left hand leaning on the hilt of his sceptre, said, "Do not seek aid, Athens, but take it;
sentences.i: So, when his eloquence had served the cause he was charged with, Aeacus — his left hand resting on the hilt of his sceptre — said: "Athens, do not ask for help. Take it.
sentences.n: "in capulo sceptri nitente sinistra" is an ablative absolute in which sinistra is the noun, the left hand, and nitente its participle. "ne petite" is a prohibition made with ne and the imperative, a poetic turn where prose would use noli petere. Athenae is vocative: the city is addressed as though it were the man standing there, and Athenae is plural in Latin, which is why the imperatives petite and sumite are plural too.

sentences.t:
nec dubie vires, quas haec habet insula, vestras
ducite; et omnia habet (rerum status iste mearum).
sentences.l: and do not hesitantly reckon the forces this island has as yours; and it has everything — this is the state of my affairs.
sentences.i: and do not hesitate to count this island's forces as your own: it has everything, and that is how my affairs stand.
sentences.n: ducere here means "reckon, count as", with vestras as a predicate accusative — not "lead". "nec dubie" is the adverb with the imperative: reckon them so, and do not hesitate about it. Magnus prints "et omnia habet"; some editions read "et o maneat", which turns the clause into a wish that this state of things may last.

sentences.t:
Robora non desunt, superat mihi miles et hosti:
gratia dis, felix et inexcusabile tempus.”
sentences.l: Strength is not lacking; there is soldiery over and above for me and for the enemy: thanks to the gods, the time is fortunate and admits no excuse."
sentences.i: Hard strength is not wanting: I have men to spare, enough for my own need and enough to meet the enemy with. Thanks be to the gods, the hour is favourable and leaves me no excuse."
sentences.n: robur is oak-timber, and so hardness, and so hardy men. superat here is "is left over, is in surplus", governing the two datives mihi and hosti — the surplus is enough for his own defence and enough to meet the enemy with; the same verb means "gets the better of" at 527. inexcusabile says that so good a moment leaves him no pretext for refusing. Magnus prints hosti; some editions read "hoc est".

sentences.t:
“Immo ita sit,” Cephalus, ”crescat tua civibus opto
urbs!” ait.
sentences.l: "Rather, may it be so," Cephalus; "I pray your city may grow in citizens!" he says.
sentences.i: "Indeed, may it be so," said Cephalus. "I pray your city may grow in citizens!"
sentences.n: immo does not deny what precedes but goes one better: yes, and more than that. Cephalus is given no verb of his own — ait comes only at the end, after the wish. opto sits inside the wish as a parenthesis, and civibus is an ablative of respect, grow in respect of citizens. The wish for citizens falls just before Aeacus tells, from 523 on, how the island lost the people it had. The edition prints a closing quotation mark where the speech resumes before crescat.

sentences.t:
“Adveniens equidem modo gaudia cepi,
cum tam pulchra mihi, tam par aetate iuventus
obvia processit.
sentences.l: Arriving just now I did indeed take joy, when a youth so beautiful, so matched in age, came out to meet me.
sentences.i: As I came in just now I felt a real gladness, when young men so handsome and so even in age came out to meet me.
sentences.n: iuventus is a collective singular, the young men of the place taken together, so its adjectives are singular where English wants plurals. "par aetate" is an ablative of respect, equal in age. equidem strengthens a first-person statement and is almost always used with "I".

sentences.t:
Multos tamen inde requiro,
quos quondam vidi vestra prius urbe receptus.”
sentences.l: Yet from that number I miss many, whom I once saw, myself received in your city before.
sentences.i: And yet among them I look for many I cannot find, men I saw when I was a guest in your city long ago.
sentences.n: requiro is not "ask" here: it is to look for something and fail to find it, and so to miss it. receptus is a passive participle agreeing with the unexpressed "I" — he was received, made a guest. The word requiro comes back in Aeacus's mouth at 521.

sentences.t: Aeacus ingemuit tristique ita voce locutus:
sentences.l: Aeacus groaned and, with a sad voice, spoke thus:
sentences.i: Aeacus groaned, and spoke in a heavy voice:
sentences.n: locutus is from the deponent loquor: passive in form, active in meaning, and its est is left out, as often. The two perfects slow the pace after the present tenses of the welcome.

sentences.t: ”Flebile principium melior fortuna secuta est.
sentences.l: A better fortune has followed a beginning to be wept over.
sentences.i: A happier fortune came after a beginning that called for tears.
sentences.n: flebilis is "to be wept over", the -bilis ending giving what can or should be done to the thing. The sentence is the shape of the whole story announced in advance: the disaster first, the remedy after — and secuta est is another deponent, active in sense. The edition prints a closing quotation mark where this speech opens.

sentences.t: Hanc utinam possem vobis memorare sine illo!
sentences.l: Would that I could recount this to you without that!
sentences.i: Would that I could tell you the one without the other!
sentences.n: utinam with the imperfect subjunctive makes a wish about the present that is known to be impossible. hanc and illo point back to the two halves of the sentence before: the better fortune he would like to tell, and the tearful beginning he cannot leave out.

sentences.t: Ordine nunc repetam.
sentences.l: Now I shall go back and fetch it in order.
sentences.i: Now I will take it up in order, from the start.
sentences.n: repetere is to go back and get a thing, and so to tell a story from its beginning rather than plunging into the middle. ordine is an ablative used adverbially, "in sequence".

sentences.t:
Neu longa ambage morer vos:
ossa cinisque iacent, memori quos mente requiris.
sentences.l: And lest I hold you up with a long roundabout: they lie bones and ash, whom you seek with remembering mind.
sentences.i: And not to keep you with a long detour: those you look for with so faithful a memory lie now as bones and ashes.
sentences.n: neu, that is neve, with the subjunctive is a negative purpose clause folded into the narrative — "and so as not to". ambages is a going-around, hence a long-drawn-out telling. "ossa cinisque" stands as the predicate: what they now are. requiris answers Cephalus's own requiro at 515.

sentences.t: Et quota pars illi rerum periere mearum!
sentences.l: And they perished — how small a part of my possessions!
sentences.i: And they were only a fraction of what I lost.
sentences.n: "quota pars" is the set idiom for how small a fraction of a whole a thing is. The subject is illi, the men, and "quota pars rerum mearum" stands in apposition to them; periere is again -ere for -erunt. The exclamation is there to warn the listener how large the coming losses are.

sentences.t:
Dira lues ira populis Iunonis iniquae
incidit exosae dictas a paelice terras.
sentences.l: A dreadful plague fell upon the people through the anger of unfair Juno, who loathed lands named after the mistress.
sentences.i: A dreadful plague fell on the people through the anger of a spiteful Juno, who hated a country named after her husband's mistress.
sentences.n: paelex is the wife's word for the other woman, and it carries her contempt: it is Juno's view of the matter, not the poem's, and what it conceals is that Jupiter carried Aegina off and she had no say in it. The lands are named for Aegina, Aeacus's mother, as 473-474 has just said. exosae is a perfect participle with active force — having conceived a hatred of — agreeing with Iunonis and governing terras, and iniqua is "unfair, ill-disposed" rather than "wicked".

sentences.t:
Dum visum mortale malum tantaeque latebat
causa nocens cladis, pugnatum est arte medendi:
sentences.l: While the evil seemed a thing of mortal origin and the harmful cause of so great a ruin lay hidden, it was fought with the art of healing:
sentences.i: As long as the evil seemed to have a mortal cause and the true source of so great a ruin stayed hidden, they fought back with the art of healing.
sentences.n: mortale here means "belonging to mortals, of human origin", not "deadly": the point is that no one yet saw a god behind it. "pugnatum est" is an impersonal passive, literally "it was fought", which English turns into "they fought". medendi is a gerund in the genitive, the art of healing.

sentences.t: exitium superabat opem, quae victa iacebat.
sentences.l: destruction was overcoming help, which lay conquered.
sentences.i: the destruction was getting the better of the remedy, and the remedy lay beaten.
sentences.n: superabat is the same verb Aeacus used at 510 in its other sense, "be left over"; here it is "get the better of". ops is help or resource, standing for the medical art of the line before. The imperfects keep the struggle going rather than closing it.

sentences.t:
Principio caelum spissa caligine terras
pressit et ignavos inclusit nubibus aestus;
sentences.l: At the outset the sky pressed the lands with thick murk and shut sluggish heats in with clouds;
sentences.i: At the outset the sky pressed down on the land with a thick fog and shut a listless heat in under the clouds.
sentences.n: principio is an ablative used adverbially, "in the beginning". caligo is a dense darkening mist rather than ordinary cloud. ignavus is "idle, doing nothing", and heat that does not move is what makes the air sick — the adjective is doing the medical work of the sentence.

sentences.t:
dumque quater iunctis explevit cornibus orbem
luna, quater plenum tenuata retexuit orbem,
letiferis calidi spirarunt aestibus austri.
sentences.l: and while four times the moon filled out her circle with joined horns, four times, thinned away, unwove the full circle, the hot south winds breathed with death-bringing heats.
sentences.i: and while four times the moon drew her horns together into a full circle, and four times waned and unwove that fullness, the hot south winds blew with deadly heat.
sentences.n: Four moons, so four months. "iunctis cornibus" is an ablative of means governed by explevit — she fills out the circle by joining her horns — and the tips of the crescent meeting is what makes the disc complete. retexuit, "unwove", answers explevit and turns the moon into weaving that is taken apart again. The austri, the south winds, were held to bring damp heat and sickness; spirarunt is a shortened form of spiraverunt.

sentences.t:
Constat et in fontes vitium venisse lacusque,
miliaque incultos serpentum multa per agros
errasse atque suis fluvios temerasse venenis.
sentences.l: It is agreed that the taint came into springs and lakes too, and that many thousands of snakes wandered through the untilled fields and defiled the rivers with their poisons.
sentences.i: It is agreed that the infection got into the springs and lakes as well, and that snakes in their thousands went wandering over the untilled fields and fouled the rivers with their venom.
sentences.n: constat, "it is agreed", opens an indirect statement, and all three verbs become infinitives: venisse, errasse, temerasse, the last two shortened from erravisse and temeravisse. vitium is a flaw or taint, and the word returns of the air at 548. temerare is to violate something that ought to be left clean.

sentences.t:
Strage canum primo volucrumque oviumque boumque,
inque feris subiti deprensa potentia morbi.
sentences.l: By the destruction first of dogs and birds and sheep and cattle, and in wild beasts, the power of the sudden disease was caught out.
sentences.i: The power of the sudden sickness was first detected in the dying of dogs, birds, sheep and cattle, and in the wild animals.
sentences.n: deprendere is to catch a thing in the act, to detect it; est is left out. strages is a laying-low, the heaped fallen. The four -que endings in a row make a list that will not stop, and Latin verse uses that piling-up where prose would put one "and" at the end.

sentences.t:
Concidere infelix validos miratur arator
inter opus tauros medioque recumbere sulco;
sentences.l: The unlucky ploughman wonders at his strong bulls collapsing in the midst of the work and lying down in mid-furrow;
sentences.i: The luckless ploughman watches in amazement as his strong bulls drop at their work and sink down in the middle of the furrow.
sentences.n: miratur takes an accusative and infinitive: he wonders at the bulls collapsing. Concidere is that infinitive, though the same ending is the poetic perfect "they fell" seen at 471 — the construction, not the form, decides it. infelix belongs to the ploughman, not to the oxen, and it is the first human grief in the plague.

sentences.t:
lanigeris gregibus balatus dantibus aegros
sponte sua lanaeque cadunt et corpora tabent.
sentences.l: as the wool-bearing flocks give out sick bleatings, both their wool falls of its own accord and their bodies waste away.
sentences.i: while the woolly flocks give out a sick bleating, the fleece drops from them of itself and their bodies waste.
sentences.n: "lanigeris gregibus ... dantibus" is an ablative absolute, which English turns into a clause. aegros properly describes the sheep, but is transferred to the sound they make — the adjective is moved onto the nearer noun, and English can keep it there. "sponte sua" means the wool comes away with no shearing.

sentences.t:
Acer equus quondam magnaeque in pulvere famae
degenerat palmas veterumque oblitus honorum
ad praesepe gemit leto moriturus inerti.
sentences.l: The horse, once keen and of great fame in the dust, falls away from his palms and, forgetful of his old honours, groans at the manger, about to die by an inert death.
sentences.i: The horse, once fiery and famous in the dust of the track, no longer lives up to his victories; forgetful of his old honours he groans at the manger, doomed to an inglorious death.
sentences.n: "in pulvere" is the dust of the racecourse, and the palma is the palm branch given to a winner, standing here for the wins themselves. degenerare with an accusative is unusual: to fall short of, to prove unworthy of. oblitus is a deponent participle, active in sense, and takes the genitive. leto inerti is a death with no action in it — the exact opposite of the life the horse had.

sentences.t:
Non aper irasci meminit, non fidere cursu
cerva, nec armentis incurrere fortibus ursi.
sentences.l: The boar does not remember to be angry, nor the hind to trust in her running, nor the bears to charge strong herds.
sentences.i: The boar forgets his rage, the hind her trust in her speed, the bears their charge on the strong herds.
sentences.n: meminit is stated once and understood in all three clauses; fido takes the ablative, cursu, of the thing relied on. Each animal loses precisely the thing it is known for, which is how the line measures the sickness.

sentences.t:
Omnia languor habet; silvisque agrisque viisque
corpora foeda iacent, vitiantur odoribus aurae.
sentences.l: Faintness holds all things; and in woods and fields and roads foul bodies lie, and the breezes are spoiled by the smells.
sentences.i: A dullness holds everything: in the woods, the fields, the roads, bodies lie foul, and the air is tainted with the stench.
sentences.n: languor is the loss of strength, the body gone slack. The three -que endings pile the places up again, as the animals were piled at 536. vitiantur is the verb of the noun vitium at 533: the same taint, now in the air itself.

sentences.t:
Mira loquar: non illa canes avidaeque volucres,
non cani tetigere lupi;
sentences.l: I shall speak wonders: dogs and greedy birds did not touch those bodies, nor did grey wolves;
sentences.i: What I shall say sounds past belief: no dogs and no greedy birds touched those bodies, and no grey wolves.
sentences.n: "Mira loquar" is a formula for announcing something the hearer will find hard to credit. tetigere is -ere for -erunt again. cani means "grey", of the wolves' coats, and it stands one line below canes, "dogs": the near-identical sound of two unrelated words is doing the work, and no English can carry it.

sentences.t:
dilapsa liquescunt
adflatuque nocent et agunt contagia late.
sentences.l: having fallen apart, they melt away, and they do harm by their breathing-out and drive contagion far and wide.
sentences.i: they fall apart, they dissolve, and they do their harm by the very breath off them, driving the infection far and wide.
sentences.n: dilapsa is a deponent participle, active in sense: having slipped apart of themselves. The subject is still the bodies of 548. adflatus is a breathing-upon: illness was understood to travel in the air a thing gives off, which is why the corpses are dangerous where nothing will eat them.
